Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 29, verses 10–11:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah"﴾. The scholars differed concerning who this verse was revealed about, giving four opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning the believers whom the polytheists took out to Badr, and they apostatized. This was related by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it was revealed concerning a people who believed with their tongues, so that when a trial from Allah or a calamity befell them in their persons and their property, they were tested. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: it was revealed concerning some hypocrites in Mecca. They used to believe, but when they were harmed and affliction from the polytheists befell them, they returned to polytheism. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: it was revealed concerning ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿah. He had embraced Islam, but feared for himself from his family and people, so he fled from Mecca to Medina, and this was before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina. His mother grieved and said to his two brothers, Abu Jahl and al-Harith, the sons of Hisham, who were her sons by the same mother: "By Allah, I will not shelter under a roof, nor eat food, nor drink drink, until you bring him back to me." So the two of them went out in search of him, found him, and kept at him until he agreed to return with them, and they brought him to her. She bound him and said: "By Allah, I will not release you from your bonds until you disbelieve in Muhammad." Then she began to beat him with whips and torment him until he disbelieved in Muhammad (peace be upon him) out of distress from the beating. So this verse was revealed concerning him. The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 29, verses 12–13:

His saying, Most High: ﴿Follow our way﴾, meaning: our religion (dīn). Mujahid said: This is the saying of the disbelievers of Quraysh to those among the people of Makkah who had believed. They said to them: "We will not be resurrected, nor will you, so follow us. If there is any burden upon you, it is upon us."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 29, verse 14–15:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people﴾. In this story there is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ, as he was informed that the prophets before him were also tested. It also contains a severe warning for whoever persists in polytheism, for although they are given respite, the people of Noah were given more respite and then they were seized.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he remained among them a thousand years, less fifty years﴾. The scholars differed concerning the lifespan of Noah, in five opinions.

The first: He was sent after forty years, and he lived among his people a thousand years less fifty years, calling them, and he lived after the Flood sixty years. This was narrated by Yusuf ibn Mihran from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: He remained among them a thousand years less fifty years, and he lived after that seventy years, so the total of his life was a thousand years and twenty years. This was said by Kaʿb al-Ahbar.

The third: He was sent when he was three hundred and fifty years old, so he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years, then he lived after that three hundred and fifty years. This was said by ʿAwn ibn Abi Shaddad.

The fourth: He remained among them three hundred years before he called them, [and he called them three hundred years], and he remained after the Flood three hundred and fifty years. This was said by Qatadah. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: he was sent at fifty years of age.

The fifth: that this verse specified the measure of his whole life. This was related by al-Mawardi.

If it is said: What is the benefit of His saying, ﴿less fifty years﴾? Why did He not say: nine hundred and fifty?

The answer: What is meant by it is to emphasise the number, and mentioning the thousand is more majestic in wording and greater as a number.

Al-Zajjaj said: The interpretation of the exception in the speech of the Arabs is emphasis. You say: "Your brothers came to me, except Zayd," so you affirm that the group came, and you exclude Zayd. Excepting half of a thing is very ugly, which the Arabs do not speak; rather, they speak of exception as they speak of deficiency. You say: "I have a dirham that is short by a qirat." If you said: "Its half is short," the better form would be to say: "I have half a dirham." Exception in the speech of the Arabs occurs only rarely among much.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then the Flood seized them﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions.

The first: death. ʿAisha narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning His saying, ﴿Then the Flood seized them﴾, that he said: "Death."

The second: rain. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and Qatadah. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is heavy rain.

The third: drowning. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Al-Zajjaj said: The flood of everything is what is abundant and encompasses the whole group. Drowning that encompasses many cities is a flood, and likewise a devastating slaughter and a sweeping death are a flood.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while they were wrongdoers﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: disbelievers.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made it﴾, meaning the ship. Qatadah said: Allah preserved it as a sign for the people on the top of al-Judi. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: It is also possible that He meant the deed He performed upon them, namely the drowning, as a sign, i.e., a lesson ﴿for the worlds﴾ [after them].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 29, verse 16–18:

Allah's statement: ﴿And Ibrahim﴾. Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj) said: it is in conjunction with Nuh (Nuh), and the meaning is: We sent Ibrahim.

Allah's statement: ﴿That is better for you﴾, meaning the worship of Allah, ﴿better for you﴾ than the worship of idols, (p-264) ﴿if you only knew﴾ what is better for you from what is worse for you. The meaning is: but you do not know.

﴿Indeed, you worship besides Allah only idols﴾. Al-Farra' (al-Farra') said: "innama" (innama, "only") in this place is a single particle and does not carry the meaning of "alladhi" (alladhi, "that which"). His statement ﴿and you fabricate a lie﴾ is linked back to "innama," like your saying: "Indeed, you only do such-and-such, and indeed you only do such-and-such." Muqatil (Muqatil) said: al-awthan (al-awthan, "idols") are the images. Ibn Qutaybah (Ibn Qutaybah) said: its singular is wathan (wathan), which is whatever was made of stone or plaster.

Allah's statement: ﴿and you fabricate a lie﴾. Ibn al-Sumayfa' (Ibn al-Sumayfa') and Abu al-Mutawakkil (Abu al-Mutawakkil) recited "wa-takhtaliquna" (wa-takhtaliquna, "and you invent") with an added tā'. There are then two opinions. Allah's statement: ﴿And if you deny﴾. This is a threat to Quraysh (Quraysh). ﴿Then nations before you have denied﴾. The meaning is: then you will be destroyed.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 29, verse 26–30:

Allah's words: ﴿So Lot believed him⦆. That is, he affirmed Abraham as true. ﴿And [Abraham] said⦆, that is, Abraham said: ﴿"Indeed, I am emigrating to my Lord."⦆ Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: "to the pleasure of my Lord." The second: "to wherever my Lord commands me." So he emigrated from the lands of Iraq to the Levant (al-Sham), and he forsook his polytheist people. ﴿And We gave him Isaac⦆ after Ishmael, ﴿and Jacob⦆ from Isaac, ﴿and We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book⦆. This is because Allah did not send any prophet after Abraham except from his lineage. ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world⦆. Concerning this there are four opinions.

The first: good remembrance, narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: good praise and a righteous offspring, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: well-being, good deeds and praise, for you will not meet anyone from among the people of the religions except that he befriends him; this was said by Qatadah. The fourth: that he was shown his place in Paradise; this was said by al-Suddi.

Allah's words: ﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter he is among the righteous⦆. Its explanation has already preceded [al-Baqarah: 130]. Ibn Jarir said: "For him there is there the reward of the righteous, not diminished in the Hereafter by what he was given of reward in this world." And what follows this has already been explained [al-A'raf: 80], up to His words: ﴿and you cut off the path⦆. Concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: that they used to ambush whoever passed by them because of their corrupt deed; this was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that when they sat in their gatherings they would pelt the wayfarer with stones, thereby cutting off the traveller's path; this was said by Muqatil.

The third: that it refers to cutting off progeny by turning away from women to men; related by al-Mawardi.

Allah's words: ﴿and you commit the evil deed in your gatherings⦆ (p-269). Ibn Qutaybah said: al-nadi (the gathering/assembly) is the majlis, and al-munkar (the evil) encompasses indecency in speech and action.

The commentators have four opinions concerning what is meant by this evil deed.

The first: that they used to mock and ridicule the people of the road, and that is the evil deed; related by Umm Hani' bint Abi Talib from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). 'Ikrimah and al-Suddi said: they would pelt with stones everyone who passed by them.

The second: wrapping the shirt around the hand, dragging the izar (lower garment), undoing the buttons, pelting and throwing with pellets, playing with pigeons, whistling, and other traits; related by Maymun ibn Mihran from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that it is breaking wind (al-diraat), related by 'Urwah from 'A'ishah, and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad explained it likewise.

The fourth: that it is having intercourse with men in their assemblies; said by Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

(p-270) This verse indicates that those who gather should not associate with one another except in ways that bring them closer to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and they should not gather for mockery and play.

Allah's words: ﴿My Lord, help me⦆, that is: by affirming my words concerning the punishment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 29, verses 31–35:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, We are going to destroy the people of this town﴾, meaning the town of Lot.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We will surely save him﴾. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim recited "la-nunajjiyannahu" and "inna munajjuka" with both letters doubled (shaddah). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i lightened both. Abu Bakr related from 'Asim: "la-nunajjiyannahu" with shaddah, and "inna munjuka" lightened, with the nun unvowelled (sakinah). The explanation of what we omitted mentioning [Hud: 77] has already been given, up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will send down upon the people of this town a punishment (rijz) from the sky﴾, and it is the pelting with stones (al-hasab) and the sinking into the earth (al-khasf).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have left of it﴾. Regarding the referent of "it" (al-makni 'anha) there are two opinions.

The first: that it is the deed (al-fi'lah) by which He dealt with them. On this view there are three sayings in the verse. One: that it is the stones which struck the earliest of this nation, said by Qatadah. The second: the black water upon the surface of the earth, said by Mujahid. The third: the report of what He did to them.

The second: that it is the town. On this view there are three sayings regarding the meaning of the verse. One: that it is the traces of their ruined dwellings, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that the verse refers to their town, which to this day has its foundations on top and its roofs below, related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The third: that the meaning is: We left it as a sign (ayah). You say, "Indeed in the sky there is a sign," meaning that it itself is the sign, said by al-Farra'.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 29, verse 38–40:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And [We destroyed] ʿAd and Thamud﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: We destroyed ʿAd and Thamud, because before this [it says] ﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it has become clear to you from their dwellings﴾, that is: it became evident to you, O people of Makkah, (p-272) from their dwellings in al-Hijaz and Yemen, a sign of their destruction. ﴿And they were [once] discerning﴾. Al-Farra' said: that is, possessors of insight. Al-Zajjaj said: They committed what they committed, and it had already become clear to them that its outcome would be their punishment. Others said: They considered themselves discerning, thinking they were upon the truth.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they could not escape [Allah]﴾, that is: they could not outrun Allah from doing to them what He willed.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So each [of them] We seized for his sin﴾, that is: We punished them for their denial. ﴿Among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of stones﴾, meaning the people of Lut. ﴿And among them were those seized by the blast﴾, meaning Thamud and the people of Shu'ayb. ﴿And among them were those We caused the earth to swallow﴾, meaning Qarun and his companions. ﴿And among them were those We drowned﴾, meaning the people of Nuh and Fir'awn. ﴿And Allah would not have wronged them﴾ by punishing them without sin, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾ by persisting in disobedience.

**The Qur'anic verse commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 29, verses 41–43:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The likeness of those who take other than Allah as protectors﴾ means the idols, which the polytheists take as protectors, hoping for their benefit and their support. Their likeness, in the weakness of their scheming, ﴿is like the spider, which takes a house﴾. Tha'lab said: "al-'Ankabut (the spider) is feminine, though some of the Arabs make it masculine." The poet said:

(p-273)

﻿[Upon their rain-cloud, from them are houses] As if the spider is the one who built them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah knows what they call upon other than Him, of anything﴾. That is, He knows what they worshipped besides Him, and nothing of that is hidden from Him; the meaning is that He will recompense them for their disbelief. ﴿And these are the parables﴾, meaning the parables of the Qur'an by which He likened the states of the disbelievers. It was said that "tilka" (these/those) here means "hadhihi" (these). ﴿Al-'alimun (those who have knowledge)﴾ are those who understand from Allah, mighty and majestic.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 29, verses 44–45:

﴿Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾, i.e., for the sake of truth (li-l-haqq), and to manifest the truth (wa-li-izhar al-haqq).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits from immorality and wrongdoing﴾. Regarding what is meant by "prayer" (al-salah) there are two opinions.

The first: it is the well-known prayer (al-salah al-ma'rufah), as said by most scholars. Anas ibn Malik narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever his prayer does not forbid him from immorality and wrongdoing, he has increased in nothing from Allah but distance."

(p-274) The second: that what is meant by "prayer" is the Qur'an, as said by Ibn Umar. What indicates this is His saying: ﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud﴾ [al-Isra': 110]. We have explained the meaning of immorality (al-fahsha') and wrongdoing (al-munkar) previously [al-Baqarah: 168; al-Nahl: 90].

Regarding the meaning of this verse, the scholars have three opinions.

The first: that when a person performs the prayer as it should be performed and reflects upon what he recites in it, it forbids him from immorality and wrongdoing; this is what it requires and necessitates.

The second: that it forbids him for as long as he is in it.

The third: that the meaning is: prayer should forbid immorality and wrongdoing.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions.

The first: and the remembrance of Allah of you is greater than your remembrance of Him. This was narrated by Ibn Umar from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and others said likewise.

(p-275) The second: and the remembrance of Allah is more excellent than everything else. This is the view of Abu al-Darda', Salman and Qatadah.

The third: and the remembrance of Allah within the prayer is greater than what He has forbidden you from of immorality and wrongdoing. This was said by Abdullah ibn Awn.

The fourth: and the remembrance of Allah of the servant, while he is in his prayer, is greater than the servant's remembrance of Allah. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 29, verse 46:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not dispute with the People of the Book except in a way that is best﴾. Regarding "in a way that is best" there are three opinions. The first: it is "There is no god but Allah." This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it is refraining from them when they offer the jizya (the poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects); if they refuse, they are fought. This was said by Mujahid. The third: it is the Qur'an and calling to Allah with the signs and proofs.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except those of them who have done wrong﴾. These are the ones who took up war and refused to pay the jizya. So dispute with these by the sword until they embrace Islam or give the jizya. ﴿And say﴾ (p-276) to whoever among them pays the jizya, when he informs you of something from their books: ﴿We believe in that which has been revealed to us and revealed to you﴾ [the verse]. Abu Hurayrah has narrated that he said: "The People of the Book used to read the Torah in Hebrew and explain it in Arabic to the people of Islam. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do not believe the People of the Book, nor disbelieve them, but say: ﴿We believe in that which has been revealed to us and revealed to you﴾ [the verse].'"

Section

There are two opinions regarding whether this verse was abrogated. (p-277) The first: it was abrogated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah﴾ up to His saying: ﴿while they are humbled﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29]. This was said by Qatadah and al-Kalbi. The second: its ruling is still in force, and this is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 29, verse 47–49:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus﴾, i.e., just as We sent down the Book to them, ﴿We have sent down to you the Book. So those to whom We have given the Book believe in it﴾, meaning: the believers among the People of the Book. ﴿And among these﴾, meaning the people of Makkah, ﴿there are those who believe in it﴾, and they are those who embraced Islam. ﴿And none deny Our signs except the disbelievers﴾. Qatadah said: denial occurs only after recognition. Muqatil said: they are the Jews.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you did not recite before it any Book﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: its meaning is, "You did not read a book before it," and "min" (from) is extra (ziyadah). As for the pronoun in "qablihi" (before it), it refers to the Qur'an. The meaning is: you were not a reader before the revelation nor a writer; and thus was his description in the Torah and the Gospel, that he is unlettered, neither reading nor writing. This indicates that what he brought is from Allah, Exalted is He.

(p-278) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Otherwise, the falsifiers would have had cause for doubt﴾. I.e., if you had been a reader and writer, the Jews would have doubted you and would have said: "This is not his description in our Book." The falsifiers (al-mubtiluna) are those who bring falsehood (al-batil), and there are two views concerning them here. One: they are the disbelievers of Quraysh, said by Mujahid. The second: they are the disbelieving Jews, said by Muqatil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Rather, it is clear signs﴾. Regarding what the pronoun refers to, there are two views.

One: it refers to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Then, concerning the meaning of the statement, there are two views. One: the meaning is, "Rather, the People of the Book's finding in their books that Muhammad ﷺ does not write or read, and that he is unlettered, are clear signs in their breasts." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Jurayj. The second: the meaning is, "Rather, Muhammad is one possessing clear signs in the breasts of those who were given knowledge from among the People of the Book, because they find him by his description and attributes," said by Qatadah.

The second: it refers to the Qur'an, and "those who were given knowledge" are the believers who memorized the Qur'an during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and after him. This community was given memorization specifically, whereas those before them used to read their scripture only by looking at it, and when they closed it they did not retain what was in it except the prophets. This is the saying of al-Hasan.

Concerning the intended meaning of "the wrongdoers" here, there are two views. One: the polytheists, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the disbelieving Jews, said by Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 29, verse 50–52:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿"Why were not signs sent down upon him from his Lord?"﴾ Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim read "āyāt" (signs) in the plural. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "āyah" (sign) in the singular. They only meant the signs like those of the prophets. ﴿Say: "Indeed, the signs are with Allah"﴾, meaning He is the one capable of sending them, and they are not in my hand. Some scholars of tafsir (the science of Qur'anic exegesis) claimed that His saying, ﴿and I am only a clear warner﴾, has been abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made clear that the Qur'an suffices as a sign from among the signs they asked for, by His saying: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book?﴾

Yahya ibn Ja'dah mentioned that: "Some Muslims came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with writings they had written, in which were some of what the Jews say. When he looked at them, he threw them away and said: 'Enough of foolishness for a people, or misguidance for a people, that they turn away from what their prophet has brought to other than themselves.'" Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them﴾ to the end of the verse.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you"﴾. The exegetes said: when they denied the Qur'an, this was revealed: (p-280) ﴿Say: "Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you."﴾ He bears witness for me that I am His messenger, and He bears witness against you for denying. Allah's testimony for him is the establishment of the miracle for him through the sending down of the Book upon him. ﴿And those who believe in falsehood﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: in other than Allah. Muqatil said: in the worship of Satan.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 29, verses 53–55:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith when he said: ﴿So rain down upon us stones from the heaven﴾ [al-Anfal: 32].

Regarding the "specified term" (al-ajal al-musamma) there are four opinions. The first: it is the Day of Resurrection; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The second: the term of life until the time of death, and the term of death until the time of resurrection; this was said by Qatadah. The third: the duration of their lifespans; this was said by al-Dahhak. The fourth: the Day of Badr; this was related by al-Tha'labi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it will surely come upon them﴾, meaning the punishment. Mu'adh al-Qari', Abu Nuhayk, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited: "wa-latatiyannahum" with the ta' (in the feminine form). ﴿Suddenly, while they do not perceive﴾ its coming.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, Hell will surround the disbelievers﴾, meaning it will encompass them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it will be said, "Taste"﴾. Ibn Kathir recited it with the nun (nuun), and Nafi' recited it with the ya' (yaa'). Whoever recited with the ya' intended the angel appointed over their punishment. Whoever recited with the nun, it is because that was by the command of Allah, Exalted is He, so it was permissible to attribute it to Him. The meaning of ﴿what you used to do﴾ is: the recompense for what you did of disbelief and denial.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 29, verses 64–66:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play.﴾ The meaning is: the life in this world is nothing but delusion that passes away quickly. ﴿And indeed, the Hereafter, that is the [true] life,﴾ meaning Paradise, ﴿if only they knew.﴾ Abu 'Ubayda said: the lam in "lahiya" (la-hiya) is an emphatic addition, and al-hayawan (the life) and al-hayat (life) are one and the same. The meaning is: it is the abode of life in which there is no death, and no disturbance (p-٢٨٤) that mars it as it mars the life of this world. ﴿If only they knew.﴾ That is: if they had known, they would have turned away from the perishable in favour of the everlasting; but they do not know.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then when they board a ship,﴾ meaning the polytheists, ﴿they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion,﴾ that is, they single Him out in supplication. Muqatil said: "al-din" (religion) here means tawhid (monotheism, the affirmation of God's oneness). The meaning is that they do not call upon those whom they associate with Him as partners. ﴿But when He delivers them [safely] to land,﴾ that is, He rescues them from the terrors of the sea and they reach the shore, ﴿at once they associate others with Him.﴾ This is a report of their obstinacy. ﴿So that they deny what We have given them.﴾ This lam is the lam of command, and its meaning is threat and warning, like His saying: ﴿Do whatever you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40]. The meaning is: that they may deny the favour of Allah in His rescuing them. ﴿And that they may enjoy themselves,﴾ Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read the lam with a sukun (lam of command, "liyatamatta'u"), on the basis that it is a command; the meaning is: let them enjoy the remainder of their lives. ﴿But they will soon know﴾ the consequence of their disbelief. The rest of the readers read the lam in "liyatamatta'u" with a kasra, and they took both lams to mean "in order that" (ka-yi), so the underlying sense is: "in order that they may disbelieve, and in order that they may enjoy themselves." The meaning of the sentence then becomes: when they associate others with Him, [it is] so that they may disbelieve and enjoy themselves; that is, there is no benefit for them in associating partners with Allah except disbelief and enjoyment of what they enjoy in the immediate life, with no share for them in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 29, verse 67–69:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have they not seen that We have made a sanctuary secure﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿that We have made a sanctuary secure﴾, meaning Makkah. We have explained this meaning in (al-Qasas: 75) (p-285). ﴿While people are being snatched away from around them﴾, that is, the Arabs were raiding one another while the people of Makkah were secure. ﴿Then in falsehood do they believe?﴾ On this there are three opinions. The first: it is polytheism (shirk), said by Qatadah. The second: it is the idols, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The third: it is Satan, said by Muqatil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿do they believe﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and 'Asim al-Jahdari recited: "tu'minun wa bi-ni'mati Allahi takfurun" with the letter ta' (taa) in both places.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and in the favor of Allah﴾, meaning: Muhammad and Islam. It was also said: it means the bounty of Allah upon them when He fed them and granted them security, ﴿they disbelieve﴾. ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah﴾, that is, claims that He has a partner and that He commanded immoralities, ﴿or denies the truth when it has come to him﴾, meaning Muhammad and the Qur'an. ﴿Is there not in Hell a residence for the disbelievers?!﴾ This is an interrogative with the meaning of affirmation (taqrir), like the saying of Jarir:

"Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts, and the most generous of the people of the world in giving wine?"

﴿And those who strive for Us﴾, that is, fight our enemies for our sake, ﴿We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾, that is, We will grant them success in reaching the straight way. It was also said: We will increase them in guidance. ﴿And indeed, Allah is with the doers of good﴾, with victory and help. Ibn 'Abbas said: by "the doers of good" he means the monotheists (muwahhidun). Others said: he means the fighters (mujahidun). Ibn al-Mubarak said: whoever finds a matter difficult, let him ask the people of the frontier posts (ahl al-thughur) about it, based on His saying: ﴿We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾.
